title: Over 3,000 Run in Chennai's Singapenn Marathon to Combat India's Cervical Cancer Crisis
excerpt: India accounts for 25% of all cervical cancer deaths worldwide, organizers say, as the marathon also promoted the national women's safety helpline.
body:
• More than 3,000 people participated in the Singapenn marathon along Chennai's Marina Beach, from Island Grounds to the Lighthouse.
  • Organizers cited that India accounts for 25% of all cervical cancer deaths worldwide, calling for urgent awareness and screening.
  • The marathon also promoted the national women's safety helpline number 1091.
  • Cervical cancer is almost entirely preventable through HPV vaccination and early screening, yet India's coverage remains limited.

3,000 Runners Along Marina Beach

The Singapenn marathon, flagged off by Singapenn Special Force (SSF) chief K. Bhavaneeswari, ran from Island Grounds to the Lighthouse along Chennai's Marina Beach on Sunday. More than 3,000 runners, walkers, and volunteers participated in the event, which combined cervical cancer awareness with a push to promote the national women's safety helpline.

Organized jointly by the Rotary Club of Madras Central, the InnerWheel Clubs of District 323, and the SSF, the marathon is part of a growing wave of community health runs in Chennai that use the format to drive public health messaging.

India's Cervical Cancer Crisis

Nallammai Ramanathan, chairman of the Singapenn Marathon, framed the event's purpose in stark terms: India accounts for 25% of all cervical cancer deaths worldwide.

"There is an urgent need for creating awareness and action against cervical cancer."

— Nallammai Ramanathan, Chairman, Singapenn Marathon

The disease is caused by persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV), which according to the World Health Organization is responsible for roughly 95% of cervical cancer cases. The cancer develops slowly and is almost entirely preventable through vaccination and regular screening — but awareness and access to both remain patchy across India.

Tamil Nadu, where the marathon was held, carries a disproportionate share of the country's cancer burden. According to the state planning commission, Tamil Nadu accounts for 6.4% of India's total cancer cases while representing only 5.6% of its population. Cervical cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer mortality among women in the state.

Strengthening Women's Safety

During the inauguration, Bhavaneeswari emphasized the marathon's twin goals: eradicating cervical cancer through awareness and strengthening women's safety through the national helpline number 1091. Sridhar Krishnaswamy, president of the Rotary Club of Madras Central, also participated in the event.

The 1091 helpline, operated by the government, provides round-the-clock assistance to women facing harassment or violence. The Singapenn Special Force, a women-led organization, has been working to raise awareness about the helpline, particularly in underserved communities.

Chennai's Growing Health Run Movement

The Singapenn marathon adds to a packed calendar of health awareness events in the city. Earlier this year, the K10K Cancer Awareness Run organized by Kauvery Hospital drew more than 12,000 participants to its fourth edition, while the Chennai Liver Foundation held its Run for Liver Health in August 2026. Community health runs have emerged as one of the most effective grassroots tools for public health messaging in Indian metro cities.

The Prevention Gap

India approved the indigenous HPV vaccine Cervavac in 2022, and the government has begun rolling it out in select states. But national coverage remains limited. Self-collection HPV testing, recently endorsed by the American Cancer Society as a valid screening option, could help expand access in India, where stigma and limited infrastructure deter many women from clinic-based screening.

Chennai has shown early initiative: the city opened a dedicated free women's cancer screening center at Thousand Lights in early 2026, equipped with mammography and Pap smear facilities. But scaling such efforts beyond metro cities remains the central challenge in India's fight against cervical cancer.
